::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Background.

Conversational agents (chatbots) are increasingly used to deliver health information to middle-aged and older adults, a population in which the determinants of technology acceptance are known to diverge from those of younger users.
However, acceptability is inconsistently defined and typically measured with ad hoc, unvalidated instruments.
The psychometrically sound chatbot measures that exist assess usability rather than acceptability or were validated in student samples.
Objective.

To develop and conduct an initial psychometric evaluation of a brief, 10-item health chatbot acceptance measure grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB).
Methods.

Twenty adults (mean age = 52.8 years, range 28-81; 85% aged 40 or older; 75% female) enrolled in a sleep-application pilot usability study completed the 10 candidate items, the System Usability Scale (SUS), and sleep measures (PROMIS Sleep Disturbance 8a; Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index).
We examined item performance, internal consistency (Cronbach's alpha),.
Conversational agents, commonly called chatbots, have moved rapidly from novelty to routine components of digital health delivery.

A scoping review of the health care literature identified 47 reports describing conversational agents used for various roles in health care (e.g., treatment and monitoring, health service support, patient education) concluded with a call for rigorous evaluation of their acceptability, safety, and effectiveness (Tudor Car et al., 2020).

text.text: Interest in these tools is driven by their scalability, their low threshold for access, and their capacity to deliver behavior-change support outside of scheduled clinical contact.

Middle-aged and older adults are a target population for this work, both because chronic disease burden concentrates in later life and because brain health and dementia risk reduction are increasingly framed as lifestyle interventions requiring sustained engagement.
However, the determinants of technology acceptance in this group may differ from those in younger people.

text.text: In summary, the result is a specific and consequential gap.
No brief, theorygrounded, psychometrically evaluated measure is available for assessing the acceptability of health-focused conversational agents among middle-aged and older adults.
This is important since this is the population in which acceptance determinants are known to diverge and the population targeted by a growing number of chatbotdelivered health interventions.

Investigators developing such interventions are left choosing between long usability instruments that measure something adjacent, acceptance scales validated in students, and locally written items with unknown properties.

We report the preliminary psychometric evaluation of a brief measure of chatbot acceptability developed and administered within a development study of Smart Learning and Engagement for Effective Personalized Sleep Using Artificial Intelligence (SLEEP-AI), a behavioral intervention incorporating a conversational agent that delivers tailored sleep-health information to people with sleep difficulties.

The measure comprises 10 items drawn from constructs central to the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) (Davis, 1989) and the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) (Ajzen, 1991), selected for brevity so that it could be embedded in a development protocol without adding excessive participant burden.

The adequacy of a sample for factor analysis depends less on the raw case-to-item ratio than on the level of communality and the degree to which factors are overdetermined (i.e., defined by several strongly loading items).

This pilot study developed a brief 10-item measure of health chatbot acceptance grounded in the TAM and TPB frameworks and examined its psychometric properties in a small sample of predominantly middle-aged and older adults.

The measure showed a coherent two-factor structure (i.e., Information Quality, Acceptance) that was invariant across rotation methods, provided high internal consistency, and produced convergent validity against an established usability instrument.

The moderate correlation between the two factors indicates that perceptions of information quality and behavioral acceptance are related but separable, consistent with the theoretical distinction between the credibility and usefulness of delivered information and the disposition to adopt and continue using the agent.
The observed structure is theoretically interpretable.
Factor 1 aligns with the TAM's dimension of perceived usefulness, extended to include the comprehension, credibility, and trustworthiness of health information.

These dimensions are especially salient when an automated agent delivers health content, and when users are older adults for whom trust and comprehension are recurrent themes in the acceptance literature (Heerink et al., 2010; Ma et al., 2021; Sou et al., 2026).
text.formatted: These dimensions are especially salient when an automated agent delivers health content, and when users are older adults for whom trust and comprehension are recurrent themes in the acceptance literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Heerink et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Ma et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Sou et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Factor 2 collapses several TPB constructs (i.e., attitude, subjective norm, perceived behavioral control, behavioral intention) into a single acceptance dimension.
That these TPB constructs did not separate empirically is unsurprising given the use of a single indicator per construct.

The subjective-norm item ("friends/family would approve") was the most complex, showing the largest secondary loading, consistent with subjective norm being the TPB construct least redundant with attitude and intention.
Although we drew items from TAM and TPB, the two emergent factors map broadly onto constructs in the Theoretical Framework of Acceptability (Sekhon et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Although we drew items from TAM and TPB, the two emergent factors map broadly onto constructs in the Theoretical Framework of Acceptability <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Sekhon et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: These included Information Quality onto perceived effectiveness and intervention coherence, and Acceptance onto affective attitude and self-efficacy.
The between-phase comparison helps explain the wide spread of scores in this small sample.

Participants in Phases 2 and 3 rated different versions of the study intervention, and both acceptance and usability were substantially higher, and less variable, in Phase 3, with effect sizes above one standard deviation.
Part of the variability in the pooled sample therefore reflects changes in the intervention rather than individual differences in disposition toward chatbots.
This has two implications.
First, it is encouraging for the measure's intended use in formative evaluation in that the scale appears sensitive to changes in the intervention participants were rating.
Further, those changes paralleled independently assessed usability on the SUS.

The items that changed most (relevance, understanding, and subjective norm) are plausibly those most affected by changes in the intervention, whereas belief and trust in the information were high in both phases and changed least.
The principal limitation of this exploratory study is the small sample (N = 20).

The conditions under which previous reports have shown that analyses using small samples may recover factor structure were met, with high item communalities and factors determined by five items each with loadings greater than 0.60 (Guadagnoli & Velicer, 1988; MacCallum et al., 1999).

text.text: Given the small sample, however, these results remain preliminary.
The very high inter-item correlations produced a near-singular correlation matrix, reflecting redundancy among the most similar items, belief and trust.
As a result, this suggests that near-duplicate items should be consolidated in a revised version of the scale.
The separation between the two factors was sensitive to a single respondent with an atypical response pattern.
With this case excluded, the subscale intercorrelation rose from r = .47 to r = .80.
The factor structure should therefore be retested in an independent sample.
Finally, the sample was drawn from a single sleep application pilot study and was demographically specific.

Although the measure is intended for middle-aged and older adults, the sample included three participants younger than 40 and eight in their 40s, and was too small to test whether the measure functions equivalently across age groups.
Generalizability to other chatbots, populations, and health domains is unknown.

Confirmatory factor analysis was not appropriate for these data since fitting a two-factor confirmatory model to the same sample that generated the structure would be circular, and the model's parameter count exceeds the available cases (Wolf et al., 2013).

text.text: The necessary next step is replication in an independent, adequately powered sample, in which the pre-specified two-factor structure can be tested to evaluate the solution found in this pilot.
A revised item set that consolidates redundant Information Quality items and strengthens the underrepresented subjective-norm content with additional items would improve the measure.

Following best-practice scale-development guidance (Boateng et al., 2018), subsequent work should add test-retest reliability, discriminant validity, and evaluation of measurement invariance across age.

text.text: An a priori power analysis for the confirmatory model, for example by Monte Carlo simulation using the present solution as the population model, may be useful in determining the sample size required for that next stage.

A brief, theory-based measure of health chatbot acceptance suggested a coherent two-factor structure, preliminary reliability, and convergent validity against an established usability scale in a pilot sample predominantly including middle-aged and older adults.

These provisional findings support the measure as a candidate instrument for formative evaluation of health chatbots in this population and provide a basis for confirmatory testing in future, adequately powered research.

Study phases.

The pilot was conducted in three sequential phases, with the application and its chatbot revised between phases on the basis of participant feedback and usage, consistent with an iterative development design.
Phase 1 (n = 7; June-July 2024) used the initial version of the application and chatbot.
The acceptance items were not part of the original protocol.

During Phase 1 it became clear that the usability measure did not capture how participants viewed the chatbot as a source of health information, and the 10 candidate items were therefore added to the assessment battery beginning with Phase 2.

All participants analyzed here (N = 20) were enrolled in Phase 2 (n = 9; September-December 2024) or Phase 3 (n = 11; August-October 2025); Phase 1 participants completed the SUS but not the acceptance items.
The intervention used in Phase 2 was a commercially-available educational website; it was abandoned because of the low usability ratings given by phase 2 participants.
The intervention used in Phase 3 included the same verbal content used in Phases 1 and 2 but was incorporated into a purpose-built WordPress website.
